Under leave-one-SL-pair-out cross-validation - our most stringent test of generalisation - the model achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.72 across ten pairs (range 0.57-0.91; mean average precision ~9%); a random train-test split gave a higher AUROC (~0.78) that we treat as an optimistic upper bound, since biomarkers and targets are shared across folds. Average precision remained low in absolute terms, reflecting the inherent challenge of predicting extremely rare resistance events (<1% of genes). Conclusions Resistance to synthetic lethal therapies arises, at least in part, from predictable patterns of network connectivity, transcriptional coordination, and context-dependent essentiality. Our integrative framework provides a computational approach for anticipating resistance mechanisms across the expanding landscape of synthetic lethal therapies, offering a foundation for designing more durable and effective combination treatments.

papers.title: PlantGeneAnn: a high-accuracy ab initio plant gene annotation tool fine-tuned from a genome foundation model
papers.abstract: Structural annotation remains a bottleneck for translating the growing catalog of high-quality plant genomes into biological insights, as current pipelines rely on RNA-seq and homologous protein evidence that are often unavailable for non-model species. Existing ab initio tools are constrained by model scale and perform poorly in complex plant genomic regions. We present PlantGeneAnn, a plant-optimized ab initio gene annotation tool fine-tuned from a genome foundation model. It combines a Mamba-MoE DNA encoder with a U-Net-style embedding decoder and a semi-Markov decoding pipeline. Trained on 40 angiosperm species, PlantGeneAnn establishes a new state-of-the-art (SOTA) across a stringent 20-species benchmark, significantly outperforming Helixer, Tiberius, and ANNEVO at exon-, intron-, and locus-levels, with mean F1 scores of 0.856, 0.880, and 0.707, respectively. It also enables efficient customized fine-tuning: LoRA fine-tuning increased the locus-level F1 of the out-of-distribution bryophyte Physcomitrium patens from 0.581 to 0.736, with performance plateauing at 40% of the fine-tuning data. Notably, PlantGeneAnn requires substantially lower peak memory usage than other baseline tools, allowing annotation of large plant genomes on standard personal workstations. PlantGeneAnn thus provides accurate, hardware-friendly ab initio annotation for diverse plant genomes, particularly newly assembled genomes, population-scale projects, and non-model plants.

papers.title: Chemical foundation models reveal molecular principles underlying glycobiology
papers.abstract: Glycans encode biological specificity through branching, linkage and stereochemical diversity, and have traditionally been modelled using specialised computational representations distinct from those developed for general chemistry. It remains unclear to what extent representations learned from general molecular chemistry capture the molecular principles of glycobiology. Here, we systematically evaluate the transfer of chemical foundation models to glycobiology using standardized benchmarks spanning taxonomy, immunogenicity, glycosylation type and protein-glycan interactions. We show that atom-level representations learned from general chemistry encode biologically meaningful molecular organization, providing particularly strong performance for molecular recognition, including immunogenicity and protein-glycan interaction prediction. Fine-tuning reorganizes these representations into latent spaces aligned with glycan architecture, glycosylation programmes and molecular recognition. Mechanistic analyses identify stereochemistry as an important determinant of successful transfer, while tokenization, context length and conformer generation influence the representation of large, branched glycans. These representations generalize from natural glycans to synthetic glycomimetics and recover experimentally validated stereochemistry-dependent glycan-lectin recognition. Together, our findings demonstrate that molecular principles learned from general chemistry are sufficient to capture fundamental features of glycobiology. They position glycans as a specialised region of chemical space and chemical foundation models as a broadly applicable framework for glycan function prediction, molecular recognition and glycomimetic discovery.

papers.title: Protein novelty, sequence similarity, and negative sampling controls reveal benchmark specific discrimination in protein protein interactionprediction
papers.abstract: Protein protein interaction (PPI) predictors are often evaluated with random pair splits that permit proteins to recur across training and test sets, while constructed negative pairs can introduce a separate source of benchmark-specific signal. We reassessed the Guo yeast benchmark using a matched protein novelty curve, independently generated MMseqs2 sequence cluster controlled R3 variants, topology only controls, degree- and length matched putative negatives, handcrafted and frozen protein language model representations, multiple model configurations, seed analyses, and connected component aware inference. In the matched R1[->]R2[->]R3 comparison, AAC+CTD-MLP ROC-AUC declined from 0.697 for seen-seen pairs to 0.626 for one-unseen pairs and 0.587 for both-unseen pairs. Across independently regenerated cluster-disjoint R3 variants at 50%, 40%, 30%, and 20% MMseqs2 clustering thresholds, performance showed no consistent monotonic trend. Guo original-negative endpoints had lower positive-network degree than positive endpoints (mean 3.34 versus 6.72), and a degree-only logistic model reached ROC-AUC 0.962 on the original negatives but 0.502 on degree-matched negatives. We used degree-matched negatives consistently for R3 training and testing; six sequence based model configurations yielded ROC-AUC 0.493- 0.547; none showed corrected connected-component-aware evidence of above-chance discrimination. A PIPR multispecies analysis reproduced degree-associated label separation but also exposed cross-species pairing as an additional pooled cue. These results show that protein novelty, operational sequence cluster separation, and negative-set topology are distinct dimensions of PPI benchmark evaluation. The Guo result is benchmark-specific and should not be generalized to sequence-based PPI prediction or protein language models overall. The dataset and source code for the experiments are publicly available at https://github.com/morufwork/guoAudit.git.

papers.title: DNA-LLM2Vec: Architecture-Aware Task-Conditioned Adaptation of Decoder DNA Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Decoder DNA foundation models pretrain with dense next-token prediction and scale to long sequences, but their representations are directional. This is a poor fit for genomic tasks that need sequence context both upstream and downstream of a locus. Bidirectional masked-language-model encoders supply this context, but they pretrain more sparsely and scale less easily to long windows. We introduce DNA-LLM2Vec, a staged decoder-to-encoder framework that opens bidirectional context, repairs the resulting mismatch with masked next-token prediction, and applies contrastive views encoding strand and positional invariance. We instantiate it on two architecturally distinct backbones, DNAGPT and HyenaDNA, and evaluate seven biological task families (grouped from GB, NT, GUE, and GUE+EPI) with frozen linear probing. The benefits of conversion are architecture-aware and task-conditioned rather than uniform. Crop-based positional contrastive learning helps most for the extended-context families (enhancer-promoter interaction and Virus-COVID), raising frozen Avg-EPI MCC to 27.5% for DNAGPT and 26.7% for HyenaDNA, whereas for shorter, local families the results depend on backbone and tokenisation. Beyond classification, bidirectional context and MNTP improve causal-eQTL variant-effect prediction specifically at distance, and a base-pair mutagenesis diagnostic shows that adaptation organises motif-aware contact structure while reverse-complement training imprints strand-consistent geometry, yet neither predicts the best downstream view. DNA-LLM2Vec therefore produces frozen bidirectional representations whose most effective adaptation view depends on the task structure and the backbone. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/semi-nothing/dna-llm2vec.

papers.title: OmniScore: Universal Scoring of Diverse Biomolecular Complexes via Equivariant Geometry-Aware Discrete Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Biomolecular structures provide a common physical basis for understanding molecular function and interactions. However, computational models typically specialize in individual molecular classes or tasks, hindering a unified representation of structural information across biological systems. Here we introduce OmniScore, a universal geometric encoder that learns shared representations of proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules and their complexes. Pretraining integrates geometric graph encoding, sequential modeling and tokenization with structural and physicochemical supervision. The frozen pretrained encoder supports complex-level model quality assessment and interaction prediction, as well as residue-level prediction, through task-specific heads. OmniScore outperforms the evaluated antibody--antigen quality-assessment baselines and also improves RNA structure ranking over baselines. For peptide-major histocompatibility complex interaction prediction, the OmniScore embeddings complement structure-prediction confidence metrics to improve predictive performance. Together, these findings support OmniScore as a shared geometric foundation for biomolecular representation and scoring across molecular classes and prediction scales, which may facilitate multi-component therapeutics development.

papers.title: From Closed-Set Annotation to In-Context Discovery: Biologically Grounded LLMs for Cellular Profiling
papers.abstract: Tumour heterogeneity reflects both cellular identity (lineage) and state (active transcriptional programs), yet computational methods generally analyse these axes separately. We introduce CellScribe, a generative framework that conditions a pretrained language model on frozen single cell foundation model embeddings through AdaLN adapters, enabling one shared model to generate an ontology- grounded cell type or a quantified meta-program profile. Supervised multitask fine- tuning produces fine grained typing across hundreds of cell types and outperforms generative and retrieval baselines on meta-program identification under study-holdout evaluation. We further train the model with reinforcement learning, scoring its generations against cell ontology distance and meta-program agreement, so that they align with biological knowledge rather than token agreement. To identify new cell types not present in the supervised training data, we post-train the model to read several labelled example cells in a single context, each conditioning its own text span, and infer the type of a query cell through in-context learning. CellScribe thus unifies cell identity and state in one generative interface, grounds both in biological structure, and identifies cell types outside the supervised vocabulary.

papers.title: PatientPheX: A Full-Text Biomedical Corpus for Patient-Specific Phenotype Information Extraction
papers.abstract: Patient-specific phenotype information extraction identifiers and normalizes phenotype entities and links them with individual patients, supporting rare disease research and genotype-phenotype analysis. However, existing datasets rarely combine full-text biomedical content with detailed annotations of patients, phenotypes, related entities, and their associations. In this work, we present PatientPheX, a corpus for patient-specific phenotype information extraction comprising 200 full-text articles, primarily case reports and case series. The corpus provides mention annotations and normalization for seven biomedical entity types, together with explicit associations between patients and entities across sentences, paragraphs, and sections. Negated findings and composite phenotype mentions are also annotated. Corpus construction combines automated pre-annotation, large language model (LLM)-assisted verification, and manual review and adjudication. Benchmarks cover entity recognition and normalization and patient-phenotype association extraction using gold-standard and predicted entities. The overall document-level entity F1 was 86.95%, while phenotype F1 was 79.33%. The best relation extraction macro-F1 decreased from 84.14% with gold-standard entities to 54.98% with predicted entities, highlighting the combined challenges of phenotype extraction and patient attribution. PatientPheX provides a resource for developing and evaluating patient-centered information extraction methods and supports the construction of structured patient-level knowledge resources for phenotype-driven biomedical research.

papers.title: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Epigenome-Wide Association Studies in the Million Veteran Program
papers.abstract: Genomic studies have improved our understanding of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) biology. Epigenetic differences in DNA methylation can reflect environmental influences, which are critical in PTSD etiology, and may additionally differentiate between PTSD cases and controls or distinguish severity of PTSD symptoms. We conducted epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) of PTSD in 22,141 subjects from the United States V.A. Million Veteran Program (MVP), using the PTSD Checklist (PCL-C), including 17,674 European ancestry (EUR), 3,430 African ancestry (AFR), and 1,037 admixed American descent (AMR) individuals. We evaluated the 17-item PCL-C and its symptom subdomains (re-experiencing, avoidance, and hyperarousal) and used our previously-reported algorithmically-defined PTSD diagnoses validated against clinical records. There were 9,413 total cases of Lifetime PTSD and 27,257 controls, with 5,184 cases and 19,382 controls in EUR, 3,095 cases and 6,240 controls in AFR, and 1,134 cases and 1,635 controls in AMR. We identified a total of 272 epigenome-wide-significant associated CpG sites across all PTSD traits, or 28 after adjusting for smoking status. We replicated 5 out of 11 CpG sites reported in a prior (Psychiatric Genomics Consortium) PTSD EWAS. There was significant enrichment of genes downregulated in somatostatin interneurons and of genes expressed in GABAergic interneurons. Regression analyses showed that PTSD case status was significantly correlated with accelerated DNA methylation aging. Contrary to previous PTSD EWAS findings, smoking status stratification suggested that the association between PTSD and methylation of the AHRR gene may be confounded by smoking status. This is the largest-scale PTSD EWAS in multiple ancestries and the first large PTSD EWAS on symptom severity. We replicate findings from previous EWAS and greatly extend knowledge of the epigenetics of PTSD.

papers.title: Measuring enteric pathogen force of infection through antibody responses in children
papers.abstract: Enteric pathogens account for a substantial global disease burden, yet population-based surveillance remains limited by the transient nature of pathogen shedding, which constrains the sensitivity of stool-based molecular testing to a narrow detection window. Detection of IgG responses in serological surveys could enable new insights into enteric pathogen transmission, but benchmarking serological measures relative to stool-based measures of infection remains a critical evidence gap. We compared measures of disease transmission in longitudinal birth cohort samples using multiplex IgG (1,601 dried blood spots, 370 children) and PCR assays (2,231 stool samples, 370 children) that overlapped for nine pathogens (norovirus GI, GII, Shigella/enteroinvasive Escherichia coli (EIEC), Campylobacter spp., enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (LT-ETEC), Salmonella enterica, Giardia spp., Cryptosporidium spp., Entamoeba histolytica). LT-ETEC and Campylobacter ranked highest while E. histolytica and S. enterica ranked lowest by both IgG and PCR measures of infection. Measures of infection were less aligned for norovirus GI, norovirus GII, Cryptosporidium, Shigella/EIEC, and Giardia. Despite this, for most pathogens, and across both measures, force of infection was lowest in the urban city of Esmeraldas and substantially higher in more rural populations, with relative risks in assay measures (seroconversion rate and PCR detected prevalence) over 2.0 for pathogens with the largest differences (Shigella/EIEC and norovirus GI). Together, our results suggest that although absolute levels of infection differed between assays, IgG and PCR captured consistent relative risk of infection across geographic strata, suggesting either method can identify high- versus low-transmission settings.

papers.title: Feasibility and Measurement Properties of a Large Language Model-Based Virtual Patient Laboratory for Clinical Reasoning Training in Physical Therapy Students: Single-Arm Pilot Study
papers.abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) configured as virtual patients may expand structured practice of clinical reasoning in health professions education. Before testing effectiveness, it must be established whether students engage with them and whether the resulting scores are complete, reliable, and related to performance with real patients. Our earlier pilot randomized trial found very low engagement with a less structured LLM-based approach. Objective: This study aimed to assess the feasibility (adherence, acceptability, and data completeness) of a revised, structured LLM-based clinical reasoning laboratory (Laboratorio de Inteligencia Artificial [LIA]) in undergraduate physical therapy education and to explore its measurement properties, including its association with clinical judgment with a real patient assessed with the Lasater Clinical Judgment Rubric (LCJR). Methods: In this single-arm pilot feasibility study, 27 third-year physical therapy students at a Spanish university completed, in 2024-2025, 3 virtual patient cases (lumbar, cervical, and thoracic spine pain) simulated by ChatGPT (GPT-4) over 4 weeks, each twice. ChatGPT scored each attempt from 0 to 4 on the same 10 dimensions of the Lasater Clinical Judgment Rubric (LCJR; 0-40 points) that human assessors applied (1-4 per dimension; 10-40 points) during a real patient encounter. Feasibility outcomes were case completion, data completeness, and satisfaction (0-10). Measurement outcomes were internal consistency and convergent validity (Spearman correlations between model-generated and human LCJR scores). Variability estimates informed the sample size of a future trial. Results: All 27 students were assessed with the LCJR; 22 (81%) completed at least 1 LIA case. Both attempts of the lumbar, cervical, and thoracic cases were completed by 78%, 63%, and 74% of students, respectively. Satisfaction data were available for 15 students (56%; mean 6.0, SD 1.3), and missing secondary data clustered in the third rotation. Internal consistency was excellent for the LCJR (alpha=.96) and ranged from .43 to .90 for model-generated ratings. Model-generated LIA scores clustered near the maximum (mean 36.0, SD 1.4). Among completers, LIA scores correlated weakly with the LCJR (rho=0.25, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.61; rho=0.44, 95% CI 0.05-0.71, when noncompleted attempts were scored as 0). Grade point average correlated almost perfectly with the LCJR (rho=0.96; n=22); after adjustment for it, the LIA-LCJR association disappeared (partial rho=-0.10). A future trial would require approximately 39 students per group (80% power, conservative variance). Conclusions: Delivering the LIA within the curriculum was feasible, but clinical judgment ratings generated by ChatGPT did not reflect those of human assessors with a real patient: they clustered near the maximum and showed no convergent validity once noncompletion was separated from performance. LLM-generated ratings should not be used as outcome or assessment measures without validation against human raters. Case calibration, completion tracking, and clarification of the GPA-LCJR relationship are also needed before a definitive trial. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06809634; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06809634

papers.title: Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST): Comparing Self-Triage Systems and Multiple Generations of OpenAI Models Against Preliminary Expert Consensus
papers.abstract: As digital self-triage becomes more widely used, quality assurance requires evaluation of both emergency recognition and overall agreement with clinical judgement, including how these outcomes differ across generations of large language models. The Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST) project intends to provide a framework to compare systems for digital self-triage against a medical 'gold standard' in Germany. In a first step developing the method and demonstrating its potential we developed a representative set of patient vignettes and compared two regulated medical-device triage systems, SmED and Infermedica, with five structured OpenAI configurations spanning multiple model generations: gpt-4.1, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-sol, and gpt-6-astra. An LLM-based patient actor covered 480 physician-curated vignettes derived from German routine triage data. A pool of seven physicians provided preliminary reference classifications and consensus for 480 vignettes. Recommendations were mapped to three urgency categories 'emergency', 'acute', and 'not urgent' and evaluated using winsorised weights derived from routine triage frequencies. Weighted emergency sensitivity ranged from 51.3% (95% CI 35.5-66.3%) for gpt-4.1 to 99.9% (99.7-100.0%) for gpt-6-astra. Weighted exact three-category agreement (accuracy) ranged from 54.4% to 68.8%; gpt-4.1 achieved the highest agreement despite the lowest emergency sensitivity. No system performed best across all urgency categories. The later-generation OpenAI configurations showed a more precautionary triage profile resembling SmED, with higher sensitivity for emergency cases; gpt-6-astra showed the strongest shift. This cross-sectional comparison across model generations suggests a shift towards more precautionary triage behaviour, without establishing a longitudinal improvement in accuracy. These findings highlight the limitations of overall agreement for evaluating self-triage and support category-specific assessment. Broader expert consensus and evaluation, as well as further steps to reduce dependence on SmED-derived source data, are needed and planned before drawing conclusions about clinical safety.

papers.title: Quantifying Cancer Clinical Trial Eligibility Using Artificial Intelligence-Based Matching
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop and validate an artificial intelligence-enabled platform that combines efficient screening with explicit eligibility logic by converting unstructured cancer trial criteria into reusable structured queries, and illustrates potential eligibility using synthetic patients. METHODS: We downloaded actively recruiting US interventional treatment trials for advanced/metastatic breast cancer, colon cancer, and non-small cell lung cancer from ClinicalTrials.gov. Medical oncologists created 24 synthetic patient vignettes. A large language model converted trial eligibility criteria into Structured Query Language (SQL) code and patient information into structured records, enabling rule-based matching without further LLM inference. Cancer details and treatment history were considered, but not laboratory results or comorbidities. Validation included physician editing of generated eligibility code for 30 trials and independent assessments by two physicians, followed by consensus adjudication, for eligibility across ten trials. We descriptively summarized potential eligibility by trial characteristics and when varying age, ECOG performance status, sex, and ZIP code. RESULTS: Of 833 candidate trials, 746 met inclusion criteria. Performing matching for all 746 trials took a median of 0.459 seconds per patient, excluding patient-data preparation. Against physician consensus, automated matching agreed on 230/240 patient-trial pairs (95.8%; sensitivity 83.3%, specificity 100%). Across synthetic patients, potentially eligible trials ranged from 10 to 258 without geographic restrictions. Counts decreased with worse performance status and geographic restriction and were relatively stable across ages 30-90. Later-phase, randomized, and molecularly selective trials generally matched fewer vignettes. CONCLUSION: LLM-generated SQL enables rapid, explicit rule-based screening for potential trial eligibility. Evaluation in synthetic vignettes supports feasibility, while missed matches underscore the need for further validation.

papers.title: DAMPA: compositionally optimised probe panel design for targeted metagenomics
papers.abstract: Probe-based enrichment enables highly sensitive direct-from-sample sequencing, and is being rapidly adopted for clinical metagenomics. Targeted metagenomics requires probe panels that capture hundreds of pathogens at comparable efficiency. However, as target sets expand, existing design methods often fail to account for genomic diversity, leading to overrepresentation of conserved sequences. The resulting composition bias reduces sensitivity precisely at the most clinically important and fast-evolving loci, such as antigenic regions, while increasing redundancy and sequencing cost. Here we show that panel composition bias can be minimised through biologically informed sequence compression. We implement the solution in DAMPA, a computationally efficient tool for metagenomic panel design. DAMPA uses pangenome graphs to compress conserved sequences while retaining genetic diversity, then designs probes from graph-node consensuses. In matched tests on six species, DAMPA successfully minimised composition bias, designing panels with up to 75.8% fewer probes than existing methods. In laboratory validation across four species, DAMPA-designed probes achieved sensitive and quantitative detection at Ct>30. In a highly diverse viral genome (Enterovirus A), where commercial panels retained only 7% of expected read depth, DAMPA-designed probes retained 44%, demonstrating improved robustness to sequence diversity and more uniform coverage. DAMPA enables rapid design of compositionally optimised panels that are cheaper to synthesise, while requiring less sequencing for complete genome coverage.

papers.title: A national ecosystem for long-read genome sequencing: Integrating population genomics and rare disease diagnostics in Sweden
papers.abstract: To evaluate the clinical implementation of long-read genome sequencing (lrGS) and establish the population reference resources needed to support its use in diagnostics, we integrate two complementary initiatives: Genome of Sweden (GoS), Sweden's contribution to Genome of Europe (GoE), and the Genomic Medicine Sweden - Rare Diseases (GMS-RD) long-read sequencing pilot. The initial GoS release of 576 individuals provides population-scale maps of genetic and epigenetic variation. Among 485 GMS-RD probands, 161 (33.2%) receive a molecular diagnosis, with lrGS providing added clinical value in 40 (24.8%). As a first-line test, lrGS could have avoided at least 42 follow-up analyses and an additional testing cycle in 7.2% of probands, reducing costs and the burden on patients. By integrating population and clinical long-read genomics, Sweden establishes a national ecosystem for genomic research and clinical diagnostics. Our findings support the clinical implementation of lrGS and offer a scalable model for national collaboration.

papers.title: BanglaDiaHallu: Hallucinations of large language models and the effect of guideline-grounded retrieval-augmented generation in Bangla diabetes question answering
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for health advice, but they can produce fluent statements that are false or unsupported, known as hallucinations, and this risk is poorly characterised in low-resource languages such as Bangla. We measured hallucinations of locally deployable open-weight LLMs in Bangla diabetes question answering and tested whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounded in Bangladeshs National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus reduces them. Forty patient questions spanning six clinical sub-domains were each answered twice, under zero-shot prompting, by Qwen3.5-9B, TigerLLM-9B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, and by BanglaDiaRAG, which adds hybrid dense (BGE-M3) and sparse (BM25) retrieval from a physician-reviewed Bangla guideline knowledge base to Qwen3.5-9B. Two physicians rated the 400 de-identified responses by consensus for medical accuracy, completeness, safety, readability and reliability on a 0-1 scale, and responses with accuracy below 0.70 were classified as hallucinated. Hallucination rates were 2.5% for Gemma-4-26B-A4B, 3.8% for TigerLLM-9B, 22.5% for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 77.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Guideline grounding lowered the rate of Qwen3.5-9B to 11.3% (difference -66.3 percentage points; 95% CI -76.3 to -55.0) and raised every criterion by 0.24 to 0.38 points (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). BanglaDiaRAG outscored Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on all five criteria and matched or exceeded TigerLLM-9B, but it remained below Gemma-4-26B-A4B in safety, readability and reliability, and its residual errors were specific, confident and potentially harmful. Guideline grounding can turn a weak general-purpose model into a much safer Bangla diabetes assistant, but the choice of base model mattered as much as retrieval and no configuration was free of hallucination, so clinical oversight remains essential before patient-facing use.

papers.title: Performance evaluation and benchmarking across 16 large language model configurations on a large real-world emergency department triage data set
papers.abstract: Background Emergency department (ED) triage is a decision process that determines patient prioritization and resource allocation. Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as decision-support tools for triage, yet most evaluations rely on curated datasets. Evidence from real-world clinical environments remains limited. The objective of this project was to evaluate the performance and reproducibility of multiple contemporary large language models for Emergency Severity Index (ESI) classification and sectoral allocation (ED vs. urgent care practice, UCP) using a real-world triage dataset. Material and Methods Retrospective cross-sectional benchmarking study conducted at a tertiary academic ED in Germany with an integrated central point of assessment (CPA). The study included all 16,107 walk-in encounters between October 18, 2023, and February 27, 2024. Sixteen configurations were compared on the first 2,000 encounters; GPT 5.1 with high reasoning effort was additionally evaluated on all 16,107 encounters. Data were collected from a structured clinical decision support system capturing presenting complaints, vital signs, and triage decisions recorded by specialized nursing staff. Results The primary outcome was the agreement between LLM-predicted and nurse-assigned ESI levels measured using quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa. Secondary outcomes included sectoral assignment agreement, misclassification patterns (over- and under-triage), confidence-agreement comparisons, and output reproducibility. In the primary analysis of all 16,107 encounters, GPT 5.1 with high reasoning effort achieved quadratic-weighted kappa = 0.5031 (95% CI 0.4904-0.5158). In the exploratory comparison of 16 configurations on the shared 2,000-encounter subset, quadratic-weighted kappa ranged from 0.180 to 0.860. The Stepwise approach, combining structured model assessments with deterministic ESI mapping, achieved quadratic-weighted kappa = 0.860 (95% CI 0.841-0.878) and 82.70% exact agreement. Most models demonstrated moderate or lower agreement. Sectoral assignment agreement (i.e. ED vs. urgent care practice, UCP) was uniformly low (kappa of 0.304 or lower). Reproducibility testing revealed substantial variability in 23% of cases, indicating non-deterministic output behavior for clinically relevant decisions. Conclusions Current large language models demonstrate heterogeneous and generally limited performance in real-world emergency triage tasks. The Stepwise approach achieved the highest agreement. Before clinical implementation, confidence estimates, reliability, and workflow integration require prospective validation in regulatory-compliant clinical settings.

papers.title: Multimodal profiling for prediction of primary resistance to anti-PD-(L)1 therapy in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer: the prospective PIONeeR biomarkers study
papers.abstract: Background Pretreatment prediction of primary resistance to anti-PD-(L)1 therapy in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains an unmet clinical need. Existing biomarkers - including PD-L1 expression and tumour mutational burden (TMB) - are insufficiently discriminatory, and multimodal predictive models targeting primary resistance are still lacking to precisely drive patients treatment strategy. Methods PIONeeR was a prospective, multicentre biomarker study conducted across 17 centres (NCT03493581). Adults with advanced NSCLC initiating standard-of-care first-line platinum-based chemotherapy plus anti-PD-(L)1 therapy, or second-or-later-line anti-PD-(L)1 monotherapy, were enrolled. Pretreatment multimodal profiling spanned six biological layers: clinical, routine medical biology, high-dimensional circulating immune phenotyping, soluble vascular markers, tumour immune contexture with digital pathology analysis of multiplex immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence, transcriptomics and genomics. The primary endpoint was prediction of primary resistance (PrR). Thirty-six feature-selection methods and ten machine learning models (360 pipelines) were benchmarked within a .632 optimism-correction framework. Results Between March 2018 and January 2023, 439 patients were enrolled (269 first-line, 170 subsequent-line); 435 were evaluable for PrR, which occurred in 39.5%. Individual biomarkers showed broad but modest associations with PrR (maximum AUROC 0.64). In the first-line chemo-immunotherapy setting, the multimodal signature achieved an optimism-corrected AUROC of 0.69 (s.d. 0.06) and a Positive Predictive Value (PPV) of 0.51 (s.d. 0.11) against a primary-resistance prevalence of 30%, outperforming PD-L1 (PPV 0.36, s.d. 0.02) and TMB (PPV 0.35, s.d. 0.03). In the subsequent-line setting it achieved an AUROC of 0.69 (s.d. 0.08) and a PPV of 0.64 (s.d. 0.08), where PD-L1 alone performed at least as well (PPV 0.68). The 18-feature signature included stromal regulatory T-cell infiltration, circulating transitional B cells, and multiple routine laboratory variables, with treatment-setting-dependent contributions. Interpretation Despite comprehensive multimodal pretreatment profiling, primary resistance to anti-PD-(L)1 therapy in advanced NSCLC cannot be captured by isolated biomarkers alone. Complete results are publicly accessible through an interactive dashboard (https://compo.inria.fr/pioneer-dashboard/), a reference resource for future meta-analyses. Multimodal integration improved risk stratification while highlighting the strong contribution of routinely available baseline variables. These findings support the development of clinically pragmatic models to identify patients who should access next-generation immunotherapy strategies aimed at overcoming primary resistance to PD-(L)1 inhibition.

papers.title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence for Cause-of-Death Assignment From Verbal Autopsy Records: A National Benchmark Study in South Africa
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Timely cause-of-death (COD) information guides health policy, yet many deaths in low- and middle-income countries are not medically certified. In Africa, fewer than 10% of deaths are. Verbal autopsy (VA) yields a structured symptom questionnaire and a free-text narrative. Mortality surveillance increasingly records the narrative alongside the questionnaire, but the algorithms used to produce VA-based statistics were designed for structured responses only, so narratives inform physician COD assignment but do not contribute to algorithmic COD assignment. We evaluated whether supervised models could use both modalities to improve COD assignment. METHODS We analyzed 4,999 VA records for deaths at ages 12 years or older from a national sample of registered deaths in South Africa (RSA), using physician-assigned CODs as the reference standard. We trained unimodal and multimodal pipelines on the labelled records: pretrained language models (PLMs) fine-tuned on narratives alone, machine learning (ML) models on structured responses alone, and the two combined at the data, feature, and decision levels. We also prompted a locally deployed generative large language model (LLM) on the same unimodal and multimodal inputs, without parameter updates. All were compared with InSilicoVA, the operational comparator representing current automated practice. We evaluated individual-level assignment, population-level agreement, calibration, and generalization across provinces in RSA, reporting these metrics rather than ranking pipelines on any one of them. RESULTS Every supervised pipeline improved on InSilicoVA by 8.5-15.9 percentage points in top-1 accuracy and 3.5-7.1 points in cause-specific mortality fraction (CSMF) accuracy. The narrative and structured pipelines performed similarly in aggregate but differed by cause: 63.9% of deaths received identical predictions, 11.6% were correct only from the narrative pipeline, and 13.6% only from the questionnaire pipeline, with the narrative pipeline more accurate for noncommunicable causes and the questionnaire pipeline for communicable causes. Against the unimodal approaches, the decision-fusion pipelines added 4.2-5.4 percentage points in top-1 accuracy, concentrated in the most common causes, whereas feature fusion with cross-modal attention improved the less common causes, adding 6.6 points (95% CI, 1.7-11.5) in balanced accuracy and 5.5 points (95% CI, 0.6-10.3) in macro F1. Feature fusion reached the highest CSMF accuracy (95.7%). Paired differences from the better unimodal representative ranged from -0.2 to +3.4 points, with all intervals including zero. The LLM exceeded InSilicoVA on individual-level metrics and reached the highest balanced accuracy of any pipeline (60.6%), while the supervised pipelines retained higher CSMF accuracy. Supervised pipelines had lower expected calibration error than InSilicoVA. Supervised gains held across all nine held-out provinces, including every top-1 comparison and nearly every macro F1 and CSMF comparison. CONCLUSIONS PLMs using narratives alone substantially improved on current best practice and matched ML pipelines using structured responses, while multiple multimodal strategies produced further gains in individual COD assignment. The zero-shot LLM showed particular strength on rare causes, whereas supervised pipelines better recovered the population cause distribution. These findings support incorporating narratives as a core input to automated VA systems and evaluating representative fusion strategies for the intended output. External validation across settings and age groups will support broader implementation.
